analysis.one_liner: Bans stock, crypto, and commodity trading by members of Congress, the president, and their families, and restricts lobbying influence.
analysis.headline: Introduced March 5, 2026 with 5 Democratic cosponsors and referred to four House committees; none has scheduled a hearing or vote, and no Republican has signed on [S1][S3][S4].
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar members of Congress, the president, the vice president, their spouses and dependent children, and candidates for federal office from buying or selling individual stocks, commodities, futures, or digital assets — money in diversified index funds and Treasury bonds would still be allowed. It would also ban former members and Senate-confirmed officials from ever lobbying for countries like China, Russia, and Iran, require spouses of senior officials to register and report paid influence work, prohibit members and their spouses from sitting on corporate boards, and extend congressional gift rules to spouses. As of now the bill has only been referred to four House committees, none of which has acted on it [S1][S2][S4].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans, who would get stricter conflict-of-interest rules for the people who write the nation's laws. Members of government would have to keep their investments in blind trusts they cannot direct, so they could no longer trade individual companies whose fortunes their votes and information can move. It would also close access channels used by foreign governments and by companies that place officials' spouses on their payrolls or pay them for influence [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary Americans affected by government conflicts of interest

how_it_helps.text: Members of Congress, the president, the vice president, candidates, their spouses and dependent children could no longer buy or sell individual stocks, commodities, futures, derivatives, or digital assets; only blind trusts, diversified publicly traded funds, and Treasury or municipal bonds would be allowed [S2]

Violating officials would have to surrender any profits and could be fined up to three times the value of the investment, paid from their own funds rather than office accounts or campaign money, and violations would be published on a public website [S2]
Former members and Senate-confirmed officials would face a lifetime ban on lobbying for China, North Korea, Russia, Iran, or other countries designated as concerns [S2]

Spouses of members and Senate-confirmed officials would have to register and file quarterly reports on paid advocacy work, with civil fines up to $200,000 and up to five years in prison for knowingly and corruptly violating the rules; members and spouses would be barred from serving on for-profit corporate boards, with current board terms grandfathered, and congressional gift rules would extend to spouses [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress, the president and vice president, their spouses and dependent children, and senior Senate-confirmed officials, who would lose the ability to trade individual securities, sit on corporate boards, and monetize their access. Lobbying and influence firms would lose a valuable roster of well-connected spouses, and former officials would lose the ability to represent adversarial foreign governments [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Lawmakers, top officials, and their families

drawbacks.text: Members of Congress and their families would have to restructure their finances around blind trusts, giving up a form of investing available to every other citizen, which critics argue could discourage qualified people from running for office [S2]

The bill leaves a major carve-out: any diversified, publicly traded fund remains permitted, and a spouse's trades as part of their own occupation are exempt, so officials and their families could still hold substantial market exposure through funds [S2]

The corporate board ban and spousal lobbying rules are grandfathered for existing board terms, and enforcement depends entirely on ethics offices and the Attorney General, whose vigor in applying the new penalties is not guaranteed [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: lawmakers and top officials give up the ability to trade individual stocks, coins, and board seats that their positions can affect, in exchange for rules that reduce the appearance and reality of officials profiting from their own decisions. The restrictions on spousal influence work and foreign lobbying close real loopholes in current law, where spouses of officials are not covered by lobbying registration. The strongest honest objection is that the rules burden innocent family members' careers alongside the officials, and the enforcement teeth depend on offices that have historically moved slowly.

outcome.mechanism: The bill has been referred to four House committees since March 5, 2026, and none of them has scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote, so it is sitting still [S4].

narrative.text: Rep. Haley Stevens (D-MI) and five Democratic colleagues introduced the No Getting Rich in Congress Act on March 5, 2026 [S1][S2][S4]
The bill was referred to the Committees on House Administration, Oversight and Government Reform, the Judiciary, and Rules, and no further action has been recorded since [S4]

The bill bans trading of individual stocks, commodities, futures, and digital assets by members of Congress, the president, the vice president, candidates, and their spouses and dependent children, allowing only blind trusts, diversified index funds, and Treasury or municipal bonds [S2]
Penalties include disgorgement of profits, fines up to three times the value of the trade, a ban on paying penalties from office accounts or campaign funds, and public posting of violations [S2]

The bill also imposes a lifetime ban on former members and Senate-confirmed officials lobbying for countries of concern like China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea, requires spouses of senior officials to register and report paid advocacy work with fines up to $200,000 or five years in prison, bars members and spouses from for-profit corporate board service with existing terms grandfathered, and extends congressional gift rules to spouses [S2]
No Republican has cosponsored the bill, which has 5 cosponsors, all Democrats [S3]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Members of Congress and senior federal officials and their families, who keep the current rules allowing them to trade individual stocks, sit on corporate boards, and have spouses do unregistered influence work. Influence and lobbying firms that sell access to officials' families also keep the status quo.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Lawmakers and their families keep the status quo

for.name: Rep. Haley Stevens
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 5, 2026, attaching new trading bans, foreign lobbying restrictions, and spousal disclosure rules to the ethics laws governing members of Congress and the executive branch [S1][S2][S4]

for.name: Reps. Tran, Salinas, Sorensen, Kaptur, and Pappas
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's five original cosponsors on the day of introduction [S2][S3]

against.name: House committee chairs (House Administration, Oversight, Judiciary, Rules)
against.role: Chairs of the four committees the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Have taken no recorded action on the bill since its referral on March 5, 2026 — no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled [S4]

against.name: House Republicans generally
against.role: No House Republican has cosponsored the bill
against.what_they_did: None of the bill's 5 cosponsors is a Republican, leaving the bill without bipartisan sponsorship roughly 11 months before this Congress ends [S3]

sides.party_line_note: All 6 members attached to the bill, the sponsor and 5 cosponsors, are Democrats, and no Republican has signed on; no votes have occurred, so the partisan shape of the full chamber is unknown.

industries.industry: Members of Congress and senior federal officials
industries.note: The bill's rules fall on the officials themselves: divest or blind-trust portfolios, surrender profits plus up to three times the trade value for violations, give up corporate board seats, and bar family members from unregistered influence work. Because these restrictions protect the public precisely at these officials' expense, their interest in stopping the bill runs directly against the public's.

industries.industry: Lobbying and influence firms, including agents for foreign governments
industries.note: The bill would end the ability of former members and Senate-confirmed officials to represent countries like China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea, and would force spouses of senior officials who sell access to register and report their clients. Firms built on placing well-connected families on client payrolls lose a product line the public currently cannot see.

industries.industry: Corporations that seat officials or their spouses on boards
industries.note: Companies would lose a channel of influence that currently puts members of Congress and their spouses inside corporate boardrooms, though sitting members' existing board terms are grandfathered. Access that is currently untracked would become reportable and then banned.

The bill allows diversified publicly traded funds, Treasuries, and municipal bonds to remain, so most retirement-style investing by officials is untouched; only individual security, crypto, and commodity trading by officials and their families is banned. The effect on the industry is modest.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in four committees with only Democratic cosponsors and no scheduled action, 11 months before the 119th Congress ends on January 3, 2027. Unless it picks up bipartisan support and a committee chair schedules a markup — which has not happened for similar proposals in recent Congresses — it will expire without a vote.
